power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 193 columns across 12 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths

**30 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `dat_reading_2errors.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/dat_reading_2errors.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_person_reading.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_person_reading.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `dat_math_2errors.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/dat_math_2errors.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_person_math.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_person_math.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_reading_robust.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_reading_robust.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_reading_robust_long.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_reading_robust_long.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_math_robust.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_math_robust.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_math_robust_long.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_math_robust_long.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_pea_reading.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_pea_reading.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd); `pes_pea_math.csv` to `anonymized_csv_data/pes_pea_math.csv` (in analysis_script_main.qmd), and 20 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 3 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: analysis_script_main.qmd, analysis_script_robustPES.qmd, analysis_script_sensitivity.qmd.

"analysis_script_sensitivity.qmd"), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 
1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("anonymized_csv_data", "anonymized_csv_data", 
"anonymized_csv_data")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)

info.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional perspectives on elementary school children's posterror slowing in reading and arithmetic

text.text: The study was conducted in line with the ethical principles of the APA and the declaration of Helsinki.
The study was also formally approved by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Human Sciences at the University of Bern (Approval No.: 2024-08-10).
All data were collected and analysed in pseudonymized form.
We wish to thank the participating children for supporting our research, their parents for consenting to children's participation, and teachers and school principals for their cooperation.
Our gratitude also goes to Stefan Kodzhabashev from the Faculty's Technology
Platform for his help with app programming and data saving, as well as to our Master students and Svenja Cibien for their help with data collection.
Children's early mathematics (basic arithmetic) and reading proficiency are among the most important academic skills for future achievement (Claessens & Engel, 2013; Duncan et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Children's early mathematics (basic arithmetic) and reading proficiency are among the most important academic skills for future achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Claessens & Engel, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Duncan et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Imagine Susie, a 4th grade student, in a test situation: when the test runs smoothly, Susie will feel certain and she will most likely speed up and promptly work herself through the test items.
However, when she encounters problems or makes a mistake as the test proceeds, Susie will hopefully detect her error, feel less confident and possibly slow down to avoid more mistakes.
As the example illustrates, a child's ability to detect errors and adapt her task strategy is crucial for test outcomes (e.g., Bellon et al., 2020; Krebs & Roebers, 2010; Steiner et al., 2019).
text.formatted: As the example illustrates, a child's ability to detect errors and adapt her task strategy is crucial for test outcomes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bellon et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Krebs & Roebers, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Steiner et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In the present contribution, one marker of children's error monitoring and adaptive strategy use that has often been overlooked will be explored in the context of reading and basic arithmetic: post-error slowing (PES; Botvinick, et al., 2001; Braver, 2012; de Mooij et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In the present contribution, one marker of children's error monitoring and adaptive strategy use that has often been overlooked will be explored in the context of reading and basic arithmetic: post-error slowing (PES; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Botvinick, et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Braver, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">de Mooij et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Traditionally, post-error slowing was investigated in adults, and the major theoretical explanation conceptualizes PES as mirroring goal-oriented, monitoring based cognitive control strategies (Botvinick et al., 2001; Braver, 2012; Moser et al., 2011; Rabbitt, 1966).
text.formatted: Traditionally, post-error slowing was investigated in adults, and the major theoretical explanation conceptualizes PES as mirroring goal-oriented, monitoring based cognitive control strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Braver, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Moser et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Rabbitt, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: PES is then thought to reflect a monitoring based, strategic upregulation of cognitive control processes following an error.
This should -ideally -have a positive effect on the accuracy of the trial following the error, that is, post-error accuracy (PEA; Botvinick et al., 2001; Laming, 1968).
text.formatted: This should -ideally -have a positive effect on the accuracy of the trial following the error, that is, post-error accuracy (PEA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Laming, 1968)</ref>.

text.text: Generally, PES occurs when overall task performance is high (> 75% accuracy), when trials are of similar difficulty, and when performance crucially depends on the balancing of speed and accuracy (Danielsmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Notebaert et al., 2009; Schroder et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Generally, PES occurs when overall task performance is high (> 75% accuracy), when trials are of similar difficulty, and when performance crucially depends on the balancing of speed and accuracy <ref type="bibr">(Danielsmeier & Ullsperger, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Notebaert et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Schroder et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: There are also other theoretical accounts of PES: Notebaert and colleagues (2009) attribute PES to increased attention to the processing of the error itself (orienting account), and Ridderinkhof (2002) proposed that PES is due to a failure of motor inhibition because of the speeded nature of responses.
text.formatted: There are also other theoretical accounts of PES: <ref type="bibr">Notebaert and colleagues (2009)</ref> attribute PES to increased attention to the processing of the error itself (orienting account), and <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Ridderinkhof (2002)</ref> proposed that PES is due to a failure of motor inhibition because of the speeded nature of responses.

text.text: Both accounts do not expect PEA to necessarily increase through PES. Danielmeier and Ullsperger (2011) showed that PES is -at least in part and depending on the task -due to trial-by-trial response threshold adjustments.
text.formatted: Both accounts do not expect PEA to necessarily increase through PES. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Danielmeier and Ullsperger (2011)</ref> showed that PES is -at least in part and depending on the task -due to trial-by-trial response threshold adjustments.

text.text: Comparing different tasks in which PES can be observed, Wessel (2012) concluded that these different accounts of PES are complementary in nature and their application may vary substantially across cognitive conflict tasks.
text.formatted: Comparing different tasks in which PES can be observed, <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Wessel (2012)</ref> concluded that these different accounts of PES are complementary in nature and their application may vary substantially across cognitive conflict tasks.

text.text: Post-error slowing can also be observed in children although it has received much less research attention.

School-aged children substantially and reliably slow down after errors, that is, show substantial PES in various multi-trial cognitive conflict tasks (Cravet & Ger, 2026; Ger & Buehler, 2024; Gupta et al., 2009; Rabbitt, 1966).
text.formatted: School-aged children substantially and reliably slow down after errors, that is, show substantial PES in various multi-trial cognitive conflict tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cravet & Ger, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ger & Buehler, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gupta et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Rabbitt, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: As to the magnitude of PES when comparing different age groups cross-sectionally, there is somewhat inconsistent evidence.

While some studies found an age-related decrease of PES magnitude over the elementary school years (Dubravac et al., 2022; Smulders et al., 2016), interpreted as finetuning and increased efficiency of PES, others reported an increase (Devervaud et al., 2020; Overbye et al., 2019), possibly indicative of improved error monitoring (see Ger & Roebers, 2024a; Masina et al., 2018; Roebers, 2022a, for no age differences within narrower age ranges).

text.text: A likely explanation for this inconsistent pattern of developmental differences is children's lack of experience with speeded cognitive conflict tasks calling, first, for the discovery of a speed-accuracy balancing strategy that, only later, becomes fine-tuned with increasing experience and age (Camerota et al., 2019; Chevalier et al., 2017; Kubota et al., 2020; Niebaum et al., 2021; Smigasiewicz et al., 2020).

text.text: Unfortunately, nearly all this work on post-error slowing and children's balancing of speed and accuracy within a task relies on classic conflict paradigms using abstract stimuli and highly uniform cognitive response demands (Camerota et al., 2019; Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Dubravac et al., 2022; van der Borght et al., 2016).

text.text: While these paradigms capture core monitoring and adaptation mechanisms, they lack the domain-specific processing requirements of academic tasks, such as reading or arithmetic.
To our knowledge, only three studies have specifically examined the development of PES in school-relevant tasks in children.

Using large-scale data from a national online learning platform with mathematics (basic and advanced arithmetic) and language "games" for primary school children, de Mooij and colleagues (2022) documented substantial post-error slowing in nearly all tasks, with PES being overall larger in arithmetic than in language activities, and with an age-related increase between ages of 5 to 9 years (but not further).

In contrast, Jacobs and colleagues (2024) assessed 2 nd and 3 rd graders' PES in the context of singledigit-multiplication tasks twice with a delay of one year and found some evidence of substantial post-error speed adjustments but no developmental changes in PES over time.

Using multiplication tasks that were adaptive to participants skills to avoid age-related differences in task performance, Jacobs et al. (2026) found substantial PES across agegroups and a linear decrease of PES between 7/8-yr-olds, 10/11-yr-olds, and 13/14-yr olds, with the latter showing comparable PES as adults.

(2026)</ref> found substantial PES across agegroups and a linear decrease of PES between 7/8-yr-olds, 10/11-yr-olds, and 13/14-yr olds, with the latter showing comparable PES as adults.

text.text: Given the sparse and inconsistent evidence of PES in elementary children's academic tasks including cross-sectional and longitudinal changes and given that PES might be a good marker for a monitoring-based strategy use in speeded multi-trial tasks, our study aimed to fill this gap by including 2nd and 4th graders, following them up over 6 months, and assessing PES in the context of simple word reading and basic arithmetic (addition and doubling).

One consequence of post-error slowing is -ideally -a reliable increase in responses' accuracy (post-error accuracy; PEA -with both PES and PEA quantified in the same task), and in adult samples, this is often, but not always found (see for example, van der Borght et al., 2016; Botvinick et al., 2001; Laming, 1968).

text.text: In children, again, the evidence is poor and mixed.
While in some developmental studies, PES was linked to PEA (Overbye et al., 2019; Pietto et al., 2023), it was not the case in others (Arnett et al., 2022; Torpey et al., 2012).

text.text: This may not be surprising given that children (a) might briefly draw their attention towards the error itself (Notebaert et al., 2009), (b) may have difficulties with the inhibition of the motor response (Ridderinkhof, 2002), or (c) may be using a certain strategy (for example, in a memory task), but their performance does not benefit from it (Bjorklund & Coyle, 1995; Miller & Seier, 1994).

text.text: Investigated under the term "utilization deficiency" (Bjorklund et al., 1997; Miller et al., 1994), it refers to a developmental phenomenon occurring in many different task types because early strategy use is effortful and resource-demanding, rendering it inefficient.

text.text: Interestingly, while de Mooij et al. (2022) found PES to be substantially related to PEA, Jacobs et al. (2024) did not observe this link although they reported significant PEA, and in Jacobs et al. (2026) study the link to performance turned out to be age-dependent. Cravet and Ger (2026) recently reported that PES assessed in the context of a cognitive conflict task was unrelated to mathematics and Italian language grades in 4th and 5th graders.

text.text: Together, these divergent findings leave the question open whether and to what extent PES is relevant for PEA and academic performance in a given task.

Two major unresolved questions were addressed in the present contribution: First, both studies provide only limited insight into cross-sectional and longitudinal developments of PES in the context of curriculum-near skills in elementary school, such as reading and arithmetic.
We therefore tackled simple word reading and basic arithmetic (addition and doubling).

Because the detection and thus the investigation of PES critically depends on the test format (two-choice answer format, timed tests) and the difficulty level (not too difficult), we opted for tablet-based tests.

Although this test format is not entirely ecologically valid, research has shown that different test formats (open-ended, multiple choice) are comparable in terms of reliability and validity (e.g., Schult & Sparfeldt, 2018; Woodcock et al., 2020) and open the possibility to investigate error detection and error-related strategies specifically.
text.formatted: Although this test format is not entirely ecologically valid, research has shown that different test formats (open-ended, multiple choice) are comparable in terms of reliability and validity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Schult & Sparfeldt, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Woodcock et al., 2020)</ref> and open the possibility to investigate error detection and error-related strategies specifically.

text.text: Shedding light on children's strategy to optimize speed and accuracy in timed tasks across age groups and over time allows testing whether monitoring-based strategies identified in laboratory paradigms generalize to academic tasks.
Simple addition and doubling problems were selected because they allowed the use of developmentally appropriate, highly standardized, and cognitively well-controlled stimuli.
These tasks also minimized linguistic and procedural demands while eliciting sufficient variability in accuracy and response times and were thus comparable to the word reading task.
Furthermore, their independence across trials allows precise measurement of trial-to-trial behavioral adjustments following errors within task blocks.

Furthermore, the response format standardizes motor responses, reduces production demands, and isolates error-related processing, thereby increasing the sensitivity of reaction-time measures to post-error adjustments rather than to peripheral task characteristics, similar to the reading task.
Second, our understanding of PES as a strategy to optimize performance (in terms of PEA) in academic contexts is very limited.

Insights into the role of PES for performance are both of theoretical and applied relevance: they provide insights into possible monitoring-based mechanisms underlying individual differences in academic performance beyond domainspecific skills (e.g., Bellon et al., 2019; Theobald et al., 2024).

text.text: And it informs innovative educational approaches targeting children's error monitoring and adaptive strategy use (Brod et al., 2020; Clerc et al., 2021).

text.text: We therefore adopted a mixed cross-sectional and longitudinal design that combines within-person change over six months with between-age comparisons of 2nd and 4th graders.

This age and time range coincides with a phase of schooling in which children typically show substantial gains in strategy use, metacognitive monitoring, and in core academic skills, including reading fluency (automated word recognition) and basic arithmetic fact retrieval (Geary, 2011; Roebers, 2017; 2022b; Roembke et al., 2019; Schwanenflugel et al., 2006; van der Ven et al., 2012), rendering these tasks well suited to investigate PES and PEA (Ger & Roebers, 2023a; Smulders et al., 2016; Schroder et al., 2019).

text.text: The inclusion of both 2nd and 4th graders allowed us to capture broader cross-sectional age-related differences across this critical range.
Moreover, the repeated measurement of PES and PEA enabled the investigation of strategy discovery and, potentially, utilization deficiency.

We expected children to show reliable post-error slowing (PES) in both simple word reading and basic arithmetic, reflecting engagement of monitoring-based performance regulation following errors (H1).

Given developmental improvements in metacognitive monitoring, strategic behavior, and efficiency of cognitive control, PES was expected to be more pronounced in 4th graders compared to 2nd graders (H2).
Furthermore, PES was expected to increase longitudinally across the school year, as growing task experience and strategy automatization should promote more consistent speed-accuracy regulation (H3).
Regarding the functional consequences of PES, we drew on the utilization deficiency literature.

Accordingly, PES was not expected to be associated with improved post-error accuracy (PEA) at the first measurement, but to emerge as performance-beneficial at the second measurement, reflecting increasing efficiency of monitoring-based strategy use (H4).
Finally, reading and arithmetic were examined as two foundational academic domains that differ in processing demands and automatization trajectories (Geary, 2011; Schwanenflugel et al., 2006).

text.text: Given the limited and inconsistent prior evidence, domain differences in PES and its relation to PEA were explored without directional hypotheses.
The data for the present study were drawn from a larger longitudinal research project conducted at the University of Bern.
Data collection took place during the 2024/2025 school year comprising three measurement occasions (see Participants and Procedure for details).
The present manuscript addresses PES and PEA in reading and arithmetic at two time points.

Although additional measures were collected (e.g., achievement motivation, executive functioning), only variables directly relevant to the current hypotheses are included to ensure a theoretically coherent and focused presentation.
The remaining measures and the third measurement point address other and distinct research questions and will therefore be reported separately.

All data were collected and analyzed in pseudonymized form.
The study was carried out in primary schools in the Bern region in Switzerland and  Classes were recruited by directly contacting school principals and class teachers.
Participation was voluntary and required written informed parental consent.
Children were informed that they could discontinue participation at any time without any negative consequences and without giving a reason.

Pilot testing of the tasks and procedure was conducted in additional classes before the first (September 2024) and second (March 2025) measurement occasions to check feasibility and to familiarize experimenters with the procedures; these pilot data were not included in the analyses.

The present study examined post-error slowing (PES) and post-error accuracy (PEA) in school-related reading and mathematics tasks.
In the following, we describe the reading and arithmetic tasks that were used at T1 and T2 to derive PES and PEA indices and included in the analyses.
Reading Task.
Reading fluency was assessed with a silent reading task.
The task was designed as a single word reading measure suitable for primary school children.

Before the main task, children received standardized spoken instructions via headphones including an example with the solution, and completed nine practice trials with feedback to familiarize themselves with the procedure.
No feedback was provided during the test trials.
On each trial, a written target word was presented above four picture options.
Children were instructed to tap the picture that matched the meaning of the word.
The three incorrect options served as distractors and were either semantically or phonologically similar to the target.
The word and pictures remained on the screen until a response was given.
The interstimulus interval was 600 ms, consisting of a 200 ms blank screen, a 200 ms fixation cross, and a subsequent 200 ms blank screen.
The assessment comprised 140 items in 2nd grade and 180 items in 4th grade, presented in a fixed order that was identical for all participants.
Accuracy and reaction times were recorded on each trial.
Arithmetic Task.
The arithmetic task was developed specifically for this study, inspired by the paradigm used by Jacobs et al. (2024).
text.formatted: The arithmetic task was developed specifically for this study, inspired by the paradigm used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Jacobs et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: It was implemented as a speeded two-choice task, providing trial-by-trial accuracy and reaction times enabling the computation of post-error slowing indices.

Each child completed 120 arithmetic problems, divided into three blocks: an addition block (36 problems; 18 without and 18 with crossing the tens boundary), a doubling block (36 problems; 18 without and 18 with crossing the tens boundary), and a mixed block ( 48problems) comprising only items below the tens boundary, some newly introduced and some repeated from previous blocks.
text.formatted: Each child completed 120 arithmetic problems, divided into three blocks: an addition block (36 problems; 18 without and 18 with crossing the tens boundary), a doubling block (36 problems; 18 without and 18 with crossing the tens boundary), and a mixed block ( <ref type="formula">48</ref>problems) comprising only items below the tens boundary, some newly introduced and some repeated from previous blocks.

text.text: In the addition and mixed blocks, the items under the ten boundary (i.e., the less difficult items) appeared first in a sub-block, thereafter the items over the ten boundary (i.e., the more difficult items) appeared second in a sub-block.
On each trial, a problem was presented along with two response options-one correct and one incorrect.
The incorrect option was designed as a distractor and was generated according to fixed rules (e.g., ±1 or ±10 relative to the correct answer), which were pseudo-randomly distributed across items.
Children responded by tapping their chosen answer on the touchscreen.

Before each test block, children received standardized spoken instructions via headphones, including an example with the solution for the addition and doubling blocks, and completed practice trials with feedback (three trials in each of addition and doubling blocks and four trials in the mixed block).
They were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.
No feedback was provided during the actual test blocks.
Task parameters were adapted to grade level.
For 2nd graders, all problems involved single-digit numbers (1-9).

For 4th graders, addition problems consisted of a two-digit number plus a single-digit number, and doubling problems involved two-digit numbers; in both cases, results were kept below 100 to maintain age-appropriate difficulty.
The presentation time of each arithmetic problem was 4,000 ms for 2nd graders and 3,000 ms for 4th graders, respectively.
After this interval, the problem disappeared, but the two response options remained visible until a response was given.
The interstimulus interval was 600 ms, consisting of a 200 ms blank screen, a 200 ms fixation cross, and a subsequent 200 ms blank screen.
PES was used as an index of monitoring-based strategy adjustments following errors.
For each task, we identified trials occurring on the next response after an error (posterror) and, for comparison, trials occurring on the next response after a correct answer (postcorrect).

PES was then computed as the difference between mean RTs on correct post-error trials and correct post-correct trials, such that positive values indicate slower responding after errors (Schroder et al., 2019):

text.text: In the arithmetic task, post-error and post-correct trial pairs were restricted to trials within the same task sub-block to avoid conflating post-error effects with difficulty transitions.
PEA was defined as accuracy on the trial immediately following an error, with postcorrect accuracy (PCA) defined analogously for trials following correct responses.
For descriptive summaries, PEA and PCA were expressed as percentage correct.
To ensure data quality and verify task comprehension, we applied accuracy thresholds based on one-sided exact binomial tests.

For the reading task (four response options; chance level = .25), cut-offs differed by version: the 2nd grade version (140 trials) required at least 45 correct responses (32.1%), and the 4th grade version (180 trials) at least 56 correct responses (31.1%).
For the arithmetic task (120 trials, two response options; chance level = .50), a minimum of 70 correct responses (58.3%) was required to perform above chance.
Cut-offs were derived using the binom.test function in R. We excluded children who performed below the cut-offs at both time points.
Based on these criteria, 2 children were excluded from the reading analyses, and 17 children were excluded from the arithmetic analyses.
Reaction times (RTs) were cleaned to remove implausible values.
Trials with RTs below 300 ms were discarded.
Upper RT limits were determined through visual inspection of the RT distributions (histograms, boxplots) and were set to 15,000 ms in arithmetic and 20,000 ms in reading.
In addition, RTs outside ±3 SD of each participant's mean RT were trimmed (computed on trials within the fixed bounds).
In the arithmetic task, participantspecific trimming parameters (mean and SD) were computed separately for each difficulty level.
This procedure led to the exclusion of 2.77% (T1) and 2.89% (T2) of reading trials and 4.46% (T1) and 4.25% (T2) of arithmetic trials.
Children were required to contribute at least one correct post-error trial at both measurement points to allow post-error calculations.
Children not meeting this criterion were excluded (2 in reading, 8 in arithmetic).
In addition, participants with fewer than two error trials were removed to ensure reliable post-error estimates (1 in reading, 14 in arithmetic).
The present analyses were conducted on complete-case samples consisting of children who completed the relevant task at both T1 and T2 and met the task-specific inclusion criteria.
To evaluate potential attrition bias, we conducted two sets of analyses.
First, we examined whether baseline (T1) task performance differed between children included in the final analytic sample and those excluded due to exclusion criteria or missing T2 data.

Wilcoxon rank-sum tests indicated no difference in T1 accuracy between included and excluded participants either for the arithmetic task (W = 23,458, p = .892), or the reading task (W = 11,258, p = .993), suggesting that initial task performance did not systematically differ between groups.
Second, we tested whether inclusion in the final analytic sample was associated with demographic variables, comparing the analytic sample to the sample with consent.

For arithmetic, Chi-square tests indicated a small but statistically significant association between grade and inclusion status (χ²(1) = 3.85, p = .050, Cramér's V = 0.074), and no significant association between gender and inclusion status (χ²(1) = 2.64, p = .104, Cramér's V = 0.061).
These effect sizes indicate that any systematic differences are small in magnitude.
For reading, inclusion status was not associated with grade, χ²(1) = 2.81, p = .094, Cramér's V = .063, or gender, χ²(1) = 0.80, p = .372, Cramér's V = .034.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that attrition and exclusion were not strongly related to baseline performance or demographic variables, although a very small graderelated imbalance in arithmetic cannot be fully ruled out.
Data were analyzed using R [version 4.6.0] (R Core Team, 2026).
No a priori power analysis was conducted because the present analyses were based on an existing longitudinal school dataset.
The sample size was therefore determined by the available cohort and by the number of children who provided valid task data after applying the predefined exclusion criteria.
We therefore focus on effect estimates and their confidence intervals when interpreting the results, particularly for attenuated or non-significant effects.

To test hypotheses 1-3, we used trial-level mixed-effects models separately for the arithmetic and reading tasks to account for the hierarchical data structure (trials nested Second, we tested whether post-error slowing was associated with post-error accuracy at the trial level.
Trial-level post-error accuracy was entered as the dependent variable in logistic mixed-effects models, coded as0 = incorrect and1 = correct.
Rather than using the aggregate PES score, we computed a local slowing index for each post-error trial.
For each child, task, grade, and measurement point, we first calculated an individual postcorrect baseline RT from correct trials following correct responses.
For each post-error trial, we then subtracted this individual baseline RT from the RT on that trial.
Positive values indicate that the child responded more slowly than their own post-correct baseline on that specific post-error trial.
The resulting local slowing scores were z-standardized within subject, grade, and measurement point and entered as predictors in logistic mixed-effects models.
Models included local slowing, measurement point, grade, and their interactions as fixed effects.
Random intercepts were included for children and classrooms to account for repeated observations within children and clustering within classrooms.
Random intercepts for items were additionally included to account for item-level differences in difficulty, allowing the baseline probability of a correct post-error response to vary across items.

Thus, the triallevel models tested whether post-error trials on which a child slowed down more strongly relative to their own baseline were associated with a higher probability of a correct response on that same post-error trial, while accounting for child-, classroom-, and item-level variability.
The linear and logistic mixed-effects models were fitted in R using `lme4` (Bates et al., 2015).

text.text: These findings indicate that developmental changes in PES should be interpreted in light of concurrent improvements in overall task performance.

The present study examined children's balancing of speed and accuracy demands, specifically their post-error adjustments, in two academic domains-reading and arithmeticunder relatively strongly controlled conditions, combining a cross-sectional (comparing 2nd and 4th graders) with a short-term longitudinal design.

We aimed to explore whether posterror slowing (PES) emerges reliably in curriculum-near tasks, how it develops over short periods of time in middle childhood, and whether it reflects efficient strategy use in terms of performance benefits.

Overall, the findings provide strong evidence that children robustly slow down after errors in both academic domains, but they also reveal task-and age-related differences in the magnitude of PES, its developmental trajectories, and functional significance which we will discuss in detail in the following paragraphs.
Consistent with our first hypothesis and in line with de Mooij et al. ( 2022), children showed clear and reliable post-error slowing in both arithmetic and reading at both measurement points.
text.formatted: Consistent with our first hypothesis and in line with de Mooij et al. ( <ref type="formula">2022</ref>), children showed clear and reliable post-error slowing in both arithmetic and reading at both measurement points.

text.text: Importantly, the substantial PES was also confirmed when PES was calculated as a drift-controlled estimate, controlling for fatigues, variations in attention, and children's actual time on task (see Supplementary Material).

These findings substantially extend prior work demonstrating substantial PES in children using cognitive conflict paradigms (Dubravac et al., 2022; Ger & Roebers, 2023a , 2023b; Gupta et al., 2009) to curriculum-near simple reading and arithmetic tasks administered in educational settings.

text.text: While often overlooked, elementary school children were found to detect their mistakes (substantial error monitoring; Botvinick et al., 2001; Braver, 2012; Roebers, 2017)  Similar to the results reported by de Mooij and colleagues (2022), PES magnitude was larger for arithmetic than for reading (see Figure 2), at both measurement points.

text.text: The somewhat larger magnitude of PES in both reading and arithmetic at the second measurement point may-at least in part -be attributable to familiarity with the task or a testretest effect.

Moreover, children's speed of working through the tasks increased, making impulsive errors more likely and short reaction times of errors may have contributed to increased PES at the end of the school year.

Admittedly, even small variations of item difficulty and the structure of the task can alter PES (Wessel, 2012) -which might have been more the case in our arithmetic than reading task (see also de Mooij et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Admittedly, even small variations of item difficulty and the structure of the task can alter PES <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Wessel, 2012)</ref> -which might have been more the case in our arithmetic than reading task (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">de Mooij et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Accurate and fast word reading followed by selecting one of four alternatives may also be structurally different from arithmetic fact retrieval (with a two-choice answering format) and therefore be less a matter of trading off speed against accuracy.
In other words, the difference in PES magnitude between reading and arithmetic may be due to distinct processing demands across domains.

Together, we interpret the robust existence of PES in both reading and arithmetic as clear indications of children's well-developed cognitive control and monitoringbased strategic regulation competencies that vary as a function of experience, task familiarity, structural features and targeted domain.
In our study, there were no consistent grade differences in PES magnitude across the two academic domains.
While in reading, there was only a tendency for larger PES in 4th graders, in arithmetic older children showed substantially stronger post-error adjustments at both measurement points.

Thus, older children in our sample appeared -at least in some cases -more sensitive to errors than younger children and this is in line with developmental progression in metacognitive monitoring, strategy use, and the accuracy-speed trade-off (Bellon et al., 2019; Brod et al., 2020; Camerota et al., 2019; Krebs & Roebers, 2010; for a review see Roebers, 2022b).

text.text: As we assume that the underlying arithmetic and reading operations are not yet fully automated in this age, children still needed to invest substantial cognitive effort to solve the task at hand.
To engage in additional cognitive control to make fine-tuned adjustments in speed, the younger children might not have enough cognitive resources remaining.
Older children, in contrast, may perform successfully as they can additionally invest in PES.

Moreover, the arithmetic task was age-adjusted and thus at a comparable difficulty level for the two age groups (while the simple word reading task was easier for the older children; see Supplementary Table S3 & S4) and the finding that 4th graders in arithmetic showed larger PES is thus consistent with evidence that PES is larger under somewhat higher task demands (de Mooij et al., 2022; Ger & Roebers, 2023a , 2024; Cravet & Ger, 2026).

text.text: Our third hypothesis concerned longitudinal change in PES.
The results suggest that PES increased in reading and arithmetic, independent of the PES measure used.

The documented increase in PES is consistent with the notion that monitoring and strategy use rapidly advance in the early elementary school years (Schneider & Löffler, 2016) and also aligns with developmental perspectives suggesting that children learn to use error signals more effectively in this age range before PES can eventually decline with further automatization (de Mooij et al., 2022; Gupta et al., 2009).
text.formatted: The documented increase in PES is consistent with the notion that monitoring and strategy use rapidly advance in the early elementary school years <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Schneider & Löffler, 2016)</ref> and also aligns with developmental perspectives suggesting that children learn to use error signals more effectively in this age range before PES can eventually decline with further automatization <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(de Mooij et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gupta et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Clearly, more longitudinal data is necessary to fully understand developmental changes.
Task repetition, school practice and familiarity of the tasks together with less frequent errors appeared to have affected children's PES magnitude, independent of age.

Interestingly, 2nd graders' PES at the second measurement point was nearly identical to 4th graders' PES at the first measurement point, suggesting that within one school year and with the re-test occasion, 2nd graders caught up with 4th graders (see Table 1, right column).

text.text: This shows that younger children can quickly learn to make fine-tuned adjustments in their strategy selection and use.
Potentially, children can be trained or coached to use PES to approach speeded, multi-trial tasks in academic domains (Ger & Roebers, 2024b).
text.formatted: Potentially, children can be trained or coached to use PES to approach speeded, multi-trial tasks in academic domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ger & Roebers, 2024b)</ref>.

text.text: The somewhat divergence of longitudinal changes in PES between the two domains suggests that developmental changes in strategic post-error adjustments are not uniform and aligns with the adult literature (Wessel, 2012).
text.formatted: The somewhat divergence of longitudinal changes in PES between the two domains suggests that developmental changes in strategic post-error adjustments are not uniform and aligns with the adult literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Wessel, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Arithmetic fact retrieval may place greater demands on monitoring and control processes during this developmental window, whereas reading fluency in relatively proficient simple word readers-particularly in transparent orthographies or highly practiced contexts-may rely more heavily on automatized processes that are less sensitive to error detection and thus PES.

Importantly, these domain-specific findings indicate that developmental changes can be detected when tasks are sufficiently sensitive, reaction time is measured at the trial level, and multiple age cohorts are included.
But again, the structural differences between the reading and arithmetic tasks may also have contributed to task-specific longitudinal changes in PES.

Moreover, at both measurement points, children were presented the identical items and it seems safe to assume that in the course of the school year, they have improved in both the simple word reading and the arithmetic tasks.

As the performance increases also mirror, experience with the task structure itself but also general practice and schooling effects in the two domains have certainly contributed to the slight increase in PES over time.

Thus, fine-tuned speed adjustments when working on academic tasks can be expected to emerge when a certain degree of competence and automatization is reached, possibly necessary prerequisites for both speeded responses and PES.
This implies for educational settings, that once children have reached a certain level of competence, teachers might target the balancing of speed and accuracy in their instructions.
The final goal of the study was to test whether PES reflects efficient strategy use and adaptive control by examining its association with post-error accuracy (PEA).
PES used as an average slowing-down was only predictive for 2nd graders, once for reading (T1) and once for arithmetic (T2).
All other links were not significant.
We interpret this finding as showing that there is no general, overall, and linear effect of PES on the task's accuracy, possibly pointing to very variable strategy use.

A child may once substantially slow down after an error, but the next error might remain undetected and response speed might remain unaffected, rendering the detection of a general benefit of PES at the mean level for performance accuracy unlikely.
The low reliability of overall averaged PES seems to support the notion of a very variable task strategy, at least in elementary school years.
Anyhow, these results have to be interpreted with caution.
In contrast, addressing local effects of PES on PEA by assessing whether PES on one trial affected PEA on this very trial, uncovered positive associations indicative of efficient strategy use.
Fourth graders' shift from a negative to a positive link in reading from T1 to T2 may be due to practice effects and hint towards overcoming a utilization deficiency.
The remaining links were positive already at T1 and did not substantially increase towards T2.

These overall positive results support the view of strategic and efficient speed and accuracy balancing in children's arithmetic and reading, enhancing subsequent performance (Bjorklund et al., 1997; Botvinick et al., 2001; Laming, 1968) -underlining its importance in academic contexts.

text.text: Thus, PES can be considered as an often overlooked but beneficial strategy, consistent with the cognitive control view that errors trigger compensatory increases in control that help prevent error repetition.
Importantly, not only were 2nd graders already able to balance speed and accuracy (see above) they seemed to rely more on slowing to improve accuracy then our 4th graders.
Older children increased their response speed while maintaining or even increasing their accuracy, thus applying a somewhat different task approach.

In reading, 4th graders' negative link between local PES and PEA at the first measurement point might suggest that slowing after errors in simple word reading does not reflect an effective strategy in fluent readers.

Such a pattern is consistent with the view that slowing may reflect attentional capturing by error (the error itself is processed and captures attentional resources and takes additional time; Notebaert et al., 2009).

text.text: Or, because 4th graders were generally reacting much faster, these might mirror impulsive errors speaking for an inhibition account (Ridderinkhof, 2002).

text.text: In fact, when reading interrupting the flow of reading after an error may be detrimental rather than beneficial for reading comprehension and thus PES might not be a productive strategy for advanced readers (see also de Mooij et al., 2022).

text.text: The fact that 4th graders' negative link between PES and PEA changed into a positive link at the second measurement might mirror a different task approach due to familiarity with the specific task demands.

Future studies may need to systematically vary the task demands to circumscribe under which conditions slowing down one's reading (after an error or when comprehension difficulties arise) might still be a valuable monitoring-based reading strategy.
Several limitations of the present study should be considered.
First, although the arithmetic and reading tasks were age-and curriculum-appropriate, they captured only specific and very constrained aspects of children's academic performance.
Second, the study focused on two discrete grades (2nd and 4th), which may limit the precision with which developmental trajectories of PES across middle childhood can be characterized.
Third, no a priori power analysis was conducted.
The sample size was determined by the available longitudinal cohort rather than by prospective power considerations.
Accordingly, nonsignificant effects should not be interpreted as evidence for the absence of an effect.
We therefore interpret attenuated or non-significant findings cautiously and focus on the precision of the corresponding estimates, as reflected in their confidence intervals.

Finally, although we accounted for grade and measurement point, individual differences in cognitive and metacognitive skills, motivation, or prior experience with speeded arithmetic and reading were not directly controlled, which may contribute to variability in PES and PEA.
Future research should examine PES across a broader range of grades, tasks, and individual characteristics to more fully understand its strategic role in academic development.

Taken together, the present findings demonstrate that post-error slowing is a robust yet often overlooked and not well understood marker of children's implicit and strategic error-related adjustments in both reading and arithmetic.

PES was found to increase over time in arithmetic and was associated with improved post-error accuracy when the local effects were considered, consistent with interpretations surrounding fine-tuned strategy use and improving micro-level cognitive control upregulations.
For reading, the effects were present but somewhat small and call for further research.
The present study helps bridge the gap between laboratory-based research and educational contexts.

We found clear evidence that already 2nd graders monitor their performance and strategically upregulate their cognitive control by selectively slowing down after errors to the benefit of their performance.

For each child, task, grade, and measurement point, we computed mean PES and mean change in PEA (post-correct accuracy -post-error accuracy in percentage) and correlated these scores separately by task, grade, and measurement point.

The current findings provide strong support for the generality of PES in childhood and establish its presence in foundational academic skills -domains in which research on children's strategy use has neglected the balancing of speed and accuracy.
From an educational point of view, more attention should be paid to children's strategy use when working under time constraints.

Some children might have more difficulties balancing speed and accuracy than others and errors may in fact occur because children work too fast or miss to adapt their speed when tasks become more difficult.
Coaching children concerning this accuracy-speed trade off may be productive in many ways.
treated as productive learning opportunities, not as failures.

Coming back to Susie in our introductory example, Susie and her classmates might need more time for the test allowing a good balancing of speed and accuracy and fostering error monitoring and correction.
Moreover, instructional practices, coaching and feedback should provide reflection prompts, motivate re-checking, and foster balancing speed and accuracy.
Error handling in reading may be better addressed outside speeded contexts, for example, through feedback and guided re-reading and should be adapted to an individual's reading proficiency.

Our findings also point to the possibility that educational classroom-based and timed assessment methods likely conflate domain-specific skills with monitoring and control processes, and performance might not yield the most valid and a pure picture of children's domain-specific learning progress.

Given PES's theoretical and practical relevance, future work should investigate the cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms underlying these domain-specific patterns of PES, strategy use and its efficiency.
